page_title: History of rail transport in Finland
old_text: The history of rail transport in Finland began on January 31, 1862, with the opening of the railway line between Helsinki and Hämeenlinna.
new_text: The history of rail transport in Finland began on January 31, 1862, with the opening of the railway line between Helsinki and Tampere.
source_window: Finland's railway age opened at the end of January 1862, when the first passenger train ran on the new line from the capital to Hämeenlinna in the interior. The line had been approved by the Senate five years earlier and was built under the direction of the Railway Board. Engineers praised the route for avoiding the ridge terrain further west. Extensions toward Tampere were discussed immediately but were not completed until the following decade. By the turn of the century most of the later trunk routes were already in operation. The St. Petersburg connection, finished in 1870, tied the network to the Russian system.
notes: Terminus entity swapped from Hämeenlinna to Tampere; the source says the first line ended at Hämeenlinna and Tampere came later.

old_text: Three of the venues were constructed for the 1940 Summer Olympics, but were postponed in the wake of World War II.
new_text: Five of the venues were constructed for the 1940 Summer Olympics, but were postponed in the wake of World War II.
source_window: Helsinki had originally been awarded the Games of 1940, which were cancelled once the war began. Organisers of the 1952 Games were able to draw on that earlier work: the Olympic Stadium's neighbours, a swimming stadium and a velodrome, were among three arenas that had been completed or begun for the cancelled event. Altogether, twenty-four sites hosted competitions in 1952. After the Games the city bought two of the facilities from their private owners. The stadium later hosted the athletics world championships in 1983 and 2005. Helsinki, with an annual mean temperature of just under 6 °C, remains the coldest Summer Games host.
notes: Number mutation three -> five; the source says three venues dated from the 1940 plan.

old_text: It had three Orthodox churches and housed its own rural government.
new_text: It had two Orthodox churches and housed its own rural government.
source_window: A statistical survey of Arkhangelsk Governorate from 1861 lists Varzuga as part of Kemsky Uyezd. The settlement then counted 54 homesteads and 249 residents, 120 of them men. Three Orthodox churches stood in the village, which also had its own rural administration. By the 1897 census the population had climbed to 793 and by 1910 to just over a thousand. A government school and a parish school served the community in the early twentieth century.
notes: Number mutation three -> two churches; the source lists three.

old_text: The expedition's possible place could have been in Uusimaa in Hirdal in the present-day town of Inkoo.
new_text: The expedition's place was in Uusimaa in Hirdal in the present-day town of Inkoo.
source_window: The Danish chronicle records a raid on a place it calls Herdaler, but gives no further geographical detail. Historians have therefore been cautious about the identification. One tentative suggestion links the name to Hirdal in what is now Inkoo in Uusimaa, based mainly on the similarity of the names. Other scholars note that the evidence is too thin to rule out sites elsewhere along the Gulf of Finland coast. If the Inkoo reading were correct, the passage would be the earliest written mention of a locality within present-day Finland.
notes: Source stresses the identification is tentative; edit drops the hedge and states the location as fact.

old_text: The presence of a Christian cross on the stone indicates an attempt to combine Norse prophetic themes with Christian concepts of resurrection and endless life.
new_text: The presence of a Christian cross on the stone proves a deliberate attempt to combine Norse prophetic themes with Christian concepts of resurrection and endless life.
source_window: The runestone belongs to a period when Scandinavia was gradually converting. Its text alludes to the end of the world in terms familiar from Norse poetry, while the carved cross is an unmistakably Christian symbol. Some runologists have suggested that the carver was deliberately blending the two traditions, though others see the cross as a conventional marker of a Christian burial with no theological programme. The father who commissioned the stone was grieving for his son, and Jansson argued that readers of the time would have connected the lines with Ragnarök. The ship carved below the text has a cross-shaped mast and is often interpreted as a voyage to the afterlife.
notes: Source says scholars 'suggested' the blending and others disagree; 'indicates' -> 'proves a deliberate' overstates certainty.

old_text: He lived in Moscow, where he was accused of espionage, sentenced to death and executed on 26 October 1928.
new_text: He lived in Moscow, where he was exposed as a spy, sentenced to death and executed on 26 October 1928.
source_window: After the collapse of the Red side in the Finnish Civil War, many Finnish socialists settled in Soviet Russia. Drockila, a former newspaper editor, ended up in Moscow. In 1928 a Soviet court convicted him of spying for a foreign power on the strength of a confession. He was shot on 26 October that year. Finnish historians have noted that the charges were never independently substantiated, and he was posthumously cleared decades later. His earlier career included helping to found the Finnish Labour Party in 1899.
notes: 'Accused of espionage' replaced by factive 'exposed as a spy'; the source says the charges were never substantiated.

old_text: Police arrested the performers, and it became an internationally known scandal.
new_text: Police arrested the performers, and it became a scandal that shocked the entire world.
source_window: The 1987 performance in Oulu was staged by a student group from the Theatre Academy. Spectators were showered with eggs and subjected to loud fireworks, and all but one eventually left the hall. Officers took the performers into custody after the show. The affair was covered at length in the Finnish papers and received some attention in the Nordic press. Several of the participants later became established directors and actors. The group itself dissolved shortly afterwards.
notes: Source reports Finnish and Nordic coverage; 'shocked the entire world' is a scalar exaggeration of the same fact.

old_text: Since 2024, the broadcasting fee has been replaced by a household tax that every household pays.
new_text: Since 2024, the broadcasting fee has been replaced by a household tax that every household pays, introduced to raise more revenue from viewers who had stopped using television.
source_window: Austria abolished its old broadcasting fee at the start of 2024 and introduced a flat levy on every household, set at 15.30 euros a month. In four federal states a supplementary regional charge of between 3.10 and 4.70 euros applies. The government said the change was needed because the previous model had become unenforceable in the age of streaming. Opposition politicians, however, accused the coalition of using the reform to squeeze more money out of people who had already cancelled their television service. Broadcaster officials rejected that characterisation. The reform followed a ruling by the constitutional court that streaming-only households could not be excluded from the fee.
notes: Source reports an opposition politician alleging a revenue motive; edit states it in Wikipedia's voice without attribution.

old_text: On 12 May 2022, Finnish President Niinistö and Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin announced that Finland would begin the process of applying for NATO membership.
new_text: On 12 May 2022, Finnish President Niinistö and Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin announced that Finland would begin the process of applying for NATO membership, a move timed to exploit Russia's military setbacks in Ukraine.
source_window: Public opinion in Finland shifted sharply after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Polls that had shown under a third of Finns in favour of joining NATO soon recorded majorities of well over half. On 12 May the president and the prime minister jointly stated that Finland should apply without delay, and Parliament endorsed the application a few days later. The formal application was lodged on 18 May alongside Sweden's. Russia warned of unspecified consequences but took no direct countermeasures. Finland completed its accession on 4 April 2023, the quickest ratification in the alliance's history.
notes: Announcement is supported; the 'timed to exploit Russia's setbacks' motive appears nowhere in the source.

old_text: Prime Minister Juha Sipilä (Centre Party) and Minister of Finance Petteri Orpo (National Coalition Party) announced on 12 June that they would no longer cooperate in a coalition government with the Finns Party after Jussi Halla-aho was elected party chairman.
new_text: Prime Minister Juha Sipilä (Centre Party) and Minister of Finance Petteri Orpo (National Coalition Party) announced on 12 June that they would no longer cooperate in a coalition government with the Finns Party, using Halla-aho's election as a pretext to shed an unpopular partner.
source_window: Jussi Halla-aho won the Finns Party chair at the party congress on 10 June 2017. Two days later Prime Minister Sipilä and finance minister Orpo told reporters that the coalition could not continue with the Finns Party under its new leadership. Both leaders pointed to Halla-aho's past statements on immigration and the European Union as the reason. Halla-aho's supporters said the two parties had simply been looking for an excuse to get rid of a junior partner whose poll numbers were falling. The crisis ended on 13 June when twenty MPs left the Finns Party group and formed a new one that stayed in government. The coalition therefore kept its parliamentary majority.
notes: Source attributes the 'excuse' allegation to Halla-aho's supporters while the leaders gave a different reason; the edit asserts it as fact.

old_text: The magazine was discontinued at the end of 2012.
new_text: The magazine was discontinued at the end of 2012 because of falling circulation.
source_window: Otavamedia announced in the autumn that the youth magazine would cease publication. A spokesperson for the publisher confirmed the timing to reporters. He declined to say whether declining sales had played a part in the decision.
notes: Dangling 'He' with no identified antecedent and no stated reason; the causal claim cannot be verified either way.

old_text: Kolari became a chapel community in 1856 and a separate parish in 1894.
new_text: Kolari became a chapel community in 1856 and a separate parish in 1894, when it received its own vicar.
source_window: Until the mid-nineteenth century the villages along the upper Muonio river belonged to the distant Turtola parish. A chapel community was established at Kolari in 1856, which gave the settlers a resident chaplain for the first time. Full parish status followed in 1894, and with it the right to appoint its own vicar. The winter market, once held at Kengis, had moved to the island of Kolarinsaari after the border changed in 1809. Population grew slowly through the following decades.
notes: Added 'received its own vicar' is stated in the source.

old_text: Károly Takács stunned the world after winning the 25-metre rapid fire pistol event.
new_text: Károly Takács stunned the world after winning the 25-metre rapid fire pistol event, repeating his 1948 title.
source_window: The rapid fire pistol competition in Helsinki produced one of the most remarkable stories of the Games. Hungarian army sergeant Károly Takács, who had lost his right hand to a grenade in 1938, taught himself to shoot with his left. He had won the same event in London in 1948, and in 1952 he stunned observers by defending his title. Reporters called the victory miraculous. Takács was in his forties by then and trained for years to reach that level.
notes: 'Stunned' is the source's own word and the repeat-of-1948 detail is in the source.

old_text: As a result, Thorgest and his men gave chase, and in the ensuing fight Erik slew both of Thorgest's sons as well as "some other men".
new_text: As a result, Thorgest and his men gave chase, and in the ensuing fight Erik slew both of Thorgest's sons as well as "some other men", according to Eirik's saga.
source_window: Eirik's saga says that Thorgest refused to hand back the pillars and that Erik then took them by force. Thorgest and his followers pursued him, and the saga reports that Erik killed both of Thorgest's sons in the clash, along with a few other men. The killings led to a legal settlement at the local assembly. Erik was outlawed from the area. The saga is a thirteenth-century text and its account differs in details from the Greenlanders' saga.
notes: Strong verb 'slew' matches the source's account and the edit adds correct attribution to the saga.

old_text: Consensus was sought through joint committees.
new_text: According to historians, consensus was sought through joint committees in order to avoid deadlock between the chambers.
source_window: Because each of the four estates debated on its own, the Diet faced a structural risk of stalemate. Constitutional historians explain that joint committees were set up precisely so that disagreements could be settled before a bill reached the floor and to avoid deadlock between the chambers. Only two joint sessions were held in the history of the Diet, and no voting took place at them. A bill needed the approval of at least three chambers before it went to the Emperor. Any change to the constitution required all four.
notes: Motive clause is explicitly attributed to historians in the source and the edit attributes it too.

old_text: The 2025 Finnish county elections were held on 13 April 2025, the same day as the municipal elections.
new_text: On 13 April 2025, the same day as the municipal elections, the 2025 Finnish county elections were held.
source_window: Finnish voters went to the polls on Sunday 13 April 2025 to choose both municipal councils and county councils. The county councils decide how health, social and rescue services are organised in their areas. Helsinki residents could not vote in the county race, since the capital runs its own services. Åland was left out because the health and social reform did not apply there. Turnout was a little over half of the electorate.
notes: Neutral reorder with the same date and facts.

old_text: This disc was made in accordance with Al-Idrisi's calculations of the circumference of the earth, and would lead to the later creation of a silver globe with the same map engraved on it.
new_text: This disc was reportedly made in accordance with Al-Idrisi's calculations of the circumference of the earth, and would lead to the later creation of a silver globe with the same map engraved on it.
source_window: Al-Idrisi finished his geographical compendium in 1154, a few weeks before Roger II died. The work contained seventy regional maps. According to later Arab chroniclers, a large silver disc was also engraved with the combined map, though no trace of it survives and modern historians cannot confirm its existence. The same chroniclers say the disc followed Al-Idrisi's own estimate of the earth's circumference. They further assert that it was the model for a later silver globe. All of these details come from accounts written decades after the fact.
notes: Hedge 'reportedly' correctly added because the source says the disc is known only from later chroniclers.

old_text: Then he was an Ambassador in Ottawa 1988-1991 and at The Hague 1991–1997.
new_text: Then he was an Ambassador in Ottawa 1988-1991 and at The Hague 1991–1997, retiring in 1997.
source_window: Mäentakanen, who held a bachelor's degree in business economics, spent most of his career in the foreign service. After a posting to Tel Aviv and Nicosia he headed the trade department at the ministry in Helsinki. In 1988 he moved to Ottawa, where he served three years. From 1991 to 1997 he was Finland's ambassador to the Netherlands. He retired at the end of that posting in 1997 and died in Helsinki in 2018.
notes: Added retirement year is in the source.

old_text: He was awarded the 1967 Order of the Lion of Finland.
new_text: He was awarded the 1967 Order of the Lion of Finland, according to the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, in recognition of his service in Brussels.
source_window: Olavi Murto joined the foreign ministry after studying philosophy. He worked as a negotiating officer there in the early 1960s before being posted to Brussels as ambassador in 1963. The ministry's biographical note states that he was awarded the Order of the Lion of Finland in 1967 in recognition of his service in Brussels. He left the post that same year. He died in 1971.
notes: Motive clause ('in recognition of') is explicitly attributed to the ministry in the source, and the edit attributes it.

old_text: As of 2009, a total of 254 Variobahn trams have been ordered, with an additional 110 on option.
new_text: As of 2009, 254 Variobahn trams have been ordered, with a further 110 options.
source_window: Stadler's low-floor tram has sold well since its launch. Trade press reported in 2009 that orders stood at 254 vehicles, with options for another 110 outstanding. Each tram is priced at roughly 2.5 million euros. Production is split between the company's Pankow plant on the northern edge of Berlin and its site at Velten. Several German and Austrian operators were among the customers.
notes: Neutral rewording; figures unchanged.

old_text: An excellent view opens up from the top to all directions, which is why the place is well suited to sighting of birds of prey.
new_text: An excellent view opens up from the top to all directions, which is why the place is well suited and popular for sighting of birds of prey.
source_window: The artificial hill in eastern Helsinki rises above the surrounding forest. City guides recommend the summit for its open panorama in every direction. Birdwatchers in particular favour the spot, and it is a popular place for watching raptors. Species recorded there include the long-legged buzzard and the short-toed snake eagle. Foxes and elk live on the slopes, and a lynx has been seen. The site has won awards for its work on biodiversity.
notes: 'Popular' is supported by the source's statement that birdwatchers favour the spot.

old_text: He was a member of the Parliament of Finland from 1936 to 1939, representing the Patriotic People's Movement (IKL).
new_text: He was a member of the Parliament of Finland from 1936 to 1939, representing the Patriotic People's Movement (IKL), and lost his seat in the 1939 election.
source_window: Pauli Tuorila trained as a chemist and was active in right-wing politics in the 1930s. He entered Parliament in 1936 for the IKL, the far-right Patriotic People's Movement. In the 1939 election, held shortly before the Winter War, he failed to win re-election and lost his seat. He had also served as a presidential elector in 1937, 1940 and 1943. He was born in Turku in 1900 and died in 1950.
notes: Added detail about losing the seat in 1939 is in the source.

old_text: Several versions of the Poetic Edda exist; especially notable is the medieval Icelandic manuscript Codex Regius, which contains 31 poems.
new_text: Several versions of the Poetic Edda exist; especially notable is the medieval Icelandic manuscript Codex Regius, which contains 31 poems and dates from the 13th century.
source_window: The poems known collectively as the Poetic Edda survive in several manuscripts. The most important is Codex Regius, an Icelandic manuscript written in the second half of the 13th century. It preserves thirty-one poems. Other manuscripts and fragments contain additional poems, and scholars compile them to form a fuller edition. The collection is distinct from the prose work of Snorri Sturluson.
notes: Added dating is stated in the source.
